Rate
rate
n. (a fixed proportion or daily allotment; the manna gathered “a certain rate every day”, the tribute Solomon received year by year, and the captive king's daily portion)
From Latin rata, in the phrase pro rata parte, according to a reckoned share, from reri, to reckon. The Hebrew is generally debar yom be-yomo, the matter of a day in its day — a phrase the Authorized Version renders variously as rate, portion, or due.

Biblical Definition

Scripture measures a great deal by the day. The manna was given so: the people were to “gather a certain rate every day” (Exodus 16:4), and the stated reason is a test — that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no. Enough for the day and no hoarding is a hard discipline, and Israel failed it in the first week. The same phrase governs the temple offerings: Solomon offered “after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts” (2 Chronicles 8:13). Worship was calendared and proportioned, not left to occasion. The word also measures tribute: the nations brought Solomon presents “a rate year by year” (1 Kings 10:25). And it closes the book of Kings on an unexpected note of mercy: Jehoiachin, released from a Babylonian prison, was given “a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life” (2 Kings 25:30). The last recorded fact about the house of David before the exile ends is that its heir was being fed daily at a pagan table.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rate as the proportion or standard by which quantity or value is adjusted, and also a settled allowance of provisions.

expand to see more

RATE, n. The proportion or standard by which quantity or value is adjusted; as, to buy at a low rate.

2. Price or amount stated or fixed on any thing.

3. Settled allowance of provisions; ration.

4. Degree; comparative height or value.

RATE, v.t. To set a certain value on; to value at a certain price or degree of excellence.

Key Scripture

Exodus 16:4 — "Then said the LORD unto Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no."

2 Chronicles 8:13 — "Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles."

1 Kings 10:25 — "And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, and armour, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year."

2 Kings 25:30 — "And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life."

Modern Corruption

Daily dependence is treated as a failure of planning, and the manna test — enough for the day, nothing hoarded — is read as poetry.

expand to see more

Exodus 16:4 says the daily rate was a test, and the thing tested was whether Israel would live by God's arrangement rather than their own. Some gathered more and it bred worms; some went out on the seventh day and found nothing. The instinct the manna exposed is universal and is not cured by prudence — Scripture praises the ant that provideth her meat in the summer, and the same Scripture forbids the barn-building of the rich fool. The distinction is not between saving and not saving but between a man whose security rests on the store and a man whose security rests on the God who gives day by day. Our Lord put the manna into the prayer He taught: give us this day our daily bread.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the corruption is one of practical unbelief, and it is at least as common in careful, provident people as in careless ones. The principle to recover is the rhythm. Scripture proportions worship by the day, the week, the month, and the year — the daily offering, the sabbath, the new moon, the three feasts — and a religion that operates only in bursts of intensity has abandoned that pattern. The final verse of 2 Kings is the quiet proof that God keeps His own rate: a captive son of David, fed every day at the table of the king who destroyed his city, and the line preserved to Matthew 1.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew debar yom be-yomo, the matter of a day in its day — Exodus 16:4, 2 Chronicles 8:13, 2 Kings 25:30; mishpat, a due or ordinance — 1 Kings 10:25.

expand to see more

Hebrew debar yom be-yomo — literally “a day's matter in its day”; the standing phrase for a daily allotment.

Hebrew aruchah — an allowance or ration; 2 Kings 25:30 of Jehoiachin's portion.

Hebrew man — manna, so named from the question “what is it?”; Exodus 16.

Hebrew nasah — to test or prove; Exodus 16:4, the stated purpose of the daily rate.

Latin rata, a reckoned share, from reri, to reckon — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“Gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them” — the manna was a test."

"“After a certain rate every day” — worship calendared, not occasional."

"“A daily rate for every day, all the days of his life” — the last verse of Kings."
